author: Benjamin Graham
biz: Put a margin of safety into your lead price

Graham never paid what something was worth; he paid a price that survived his own mistakes. Take your two brands and work out the maximum cost per lead that still leaves a profit if your phone and WhatsApp conversion rate fell by a third and your lender payout slipped. That number, not your current average, is your bid ceiling on Google, Bing and Facebook. Set it this week and measure cost per completed case rather than cost per lead, broken down by source, so you can see which channels only look affordable while conversion happens to be good.

Graham's edge was opening documents everyone could see and nobody read. Your equivalent is the raw record of what actually happens after the lead arrives: call recordings, WhatsApp threads, the cases that drop out, the Debt Support Direct clients who disengage. Pick ten files this week at random across both businesses, read them end to end, and record two things: whether the customer clearly understood the broker fee and that approval is never guaranteed, and whether any sign of vulnerability was spotted and acted on. Measure the percentage of files where both are evidenced, and track it monthly as Consumer Duty outcome evidence.

b: Benjamin Grossbaum was born in London on the ninth of May 1894, and he was barely a year old when his parents carried him across the Atlantic to New York. His father ran the American end of the family business, importing china and ornaments, the sort of delicate stock that sells only when people feel comfortable enough to buy pretty things. For a while the family was comfortable too. There was a maid, a cook, a governess.

Then, when Benjamin was nine, his father died. The business went with him. His mother Dorothy turned the family home into a boarding house and took in lodgers, and the household slid out of the middle class into something much thinner and far more anxious.

What happened next is the thing the whole of Graham's later life argues with. Looking for a way back, his mother borrowed money to buy shares in United States Steel on margin, which is to say she put down a fraction of the price and owed the rest. In the autumn of 1907 the American banking system seized up, share prices collapsed, and the loan was called in. She was wiped out.

Graham remembered one detail more sharply than the loss itself. Sent to the bank to cash a cheque, he stood at the window and heard the teller call across to the cashier, asking whether Dorothy Grossbaum was good for five dollars. He was a boy in short trousers. He understood every word of it.

Two ideas were planted in that house, and he spent fifty years unpacking them. The first is that borrowed money turns a temporary fall in price into a permanent loss of capital. The second is quieter and larger. A share of United States Steel was a claim on the same steel company the day after the panic as the day before. Only the price had changed. The gap between those two facts became his life's work.

b: School was the one thing in his life that still worked. Graham went to Boys High School in Brooklyn and read with the appetite of someone using books as an escape route, Latin and Greek, mathematics and poetry. He won a scholarship to Columbia, then a clerical mistake at the college lost it, and he spent a year taking whatever paid work he could find before sitting the examination again and winning the place a second time.

He was sixteen when he finally walked in, and he graduated in 1914 in three and a half years rather than four, second in his year. Then the university did something unusual. Before his final term was out, three separate departments offered him a teaching post: mathematics, English and philosophy. A twenty year old was being invited to choose which kind of mind he wanted to spend his life being.

He turned down all three. His mother still needed supporting and an instructor's salary would not stretch. So he went to the dean of the college, Frederick Keppel, and asked for help finding work that actually paid. Keppel sent him downtown to a small brokerage house called Newburger, Henderson and Loeb.

It is worth pausing on what Wall Street was in 1914, because it explains why Graham's contribution looks obvious now and was so peculiar then. Disclosure by industrial companies was thin and largely voluntary. Men bought shares on tips, on the reputation of the promoters behind them, on the movement of the ticker tape. Figures existed, buried in filings and annual reports, and almost nobody read them. Nobody had written down a method for deciding what a business was actually worth.
The classical scholar who could not afford to be a classical scholar had just been handed a subject with no textbook.

ch.h: The Boy Who Was Offered Three Chairs

b: His first job was to chalk prices on a board and run messages, for something close to twelve dollars a week. Within months he was writing descriptions of bonds, and his useful trait showed itself at once. He actually read the documents. When other men wanted to know whether a railroad could cover its interest, Graham went and found the filings and worked it out.

Here he met the raw material nobody exploited. Railroads and pipelines, unlike ordinary companies, were obliged by law to file detailed annual reports with the Interstate Commerce Commission in Washington. Those filings sat in a government library, public and almost entirely unread, setting out assets, cash and bond holdings line by line, often bearing no relation to the price of the shares.

By 1920 he was a partner. By 1923 he was running money himself, and on the first day of 1926 he opened the Benjamin Graham Joint Account with about four hundred and fifty thousand dollars. Much of what he did was not glamorous. He bought one security and sold a related one short, pocketing the difference between two prices that ought to have been the same, an operation known as arbitrage. He hunted companies trading for less than the cash in their own tills.

Out of this came the distinction he would hammer at for the rest of his life, and which he later wrote down almost as a legal definition. An investment operation is one which, on thorough analysis, promises safety of principal and an adequate return. Everything else is speculation.

Read that slowly, because it has no reference in it to how clever you are, how confident you feel, or how the shares have moved lately. It asks two questions only. Have you done the work, and can you afford to be wrong.

b: In 1926 Graham was in the Commission's library in Washington going through pipeline filings, and he found Northern Pipe Line. It was one of eight pipeline companies cut loose from Standard Oil when the courts broke up the trust in 1911. Its shares traded at about sixty two dollars.

The filing told a different story. The tangible assets came to something like eighty two dollars a share, and a large part of that was not pipe or pumping stations but high grade railroad bonds sitting idle on the balance sheet. Add a reasonable value for the operating business and Graham reckoned the shares were worth close to ninety five dollars. The company was carrying a fortune it was not using, and the market priced it as though the fortune were not there.

There were only forty thousand shares in existence. Over about a year Graham quietly bought two thousand of them, then went to the annual meeting in January 1927 and proposed, politely and in writing, that the bonds be sold and the surplus handed back to the owners of the company.
Nobody seconded his motion. Under the rules that meant his memorandum could not even be read aloud. The meeting was adjourned and he was shown out.

So he did the slow thing. He bought more shares and spent a year writing to other shareholders asking them to lend him their votes. At the 1928 meeting he arrived holding proxies for about thirty eight per cent of the company and used them to put two directors on the board. Within weeks the management agreed to liquidate the bonds and distribute seventy dollars a share,.
The lesson is not that activism pays. It is the one underneath. A share is not a betting slip. It is a piece of a real business, and an owner is entitled to ask what is in the safe.

b: By 1929 Graham was thirty five, admired, and in his own later judgement overconfident. He had been right about a great deal, and being right had made him careless about the one thing he had learned as a child. The Joint Account was carrying borrowed money, something close to forty four per cent of its value in margin debt.

What followed was not one crash but four years of them. By the figures the writer James Grant assembled, the account fell about twenty per cent in 1929, about fifty per cent in 1930, sixteen per cent in 1931 and two per cent in 1932. Against the peak, roughly thirty cents of every dollar was left. The broad market did slightly worse.

Graham had bought cheap companies and done the analysis, and it had not saved him, because cheap can become cheaper and leverage does not wait for you to be proved right. His partner Jerome Newman's family put money in to keep the firm alive. Graham took no profit share for years, working until his investors were made whole, which happened around 1935.

He also learned something about himself that he set down later with unusual flatness. He had thought the danger was being wrong about a business. The real danger was being right about a business and not surviving long enough to collect.

This is where the most famous phrase in investing was actually forged. Margin of safety does not mean buying good things. It means buying them at a price low enough that your estimate can be wrong, the world can turn against you, and you are still standing. A bridge rated for thirty tons is not built because anyone plans to drive a thirty ton lorry across it.

b: In 1928, with the firm still intact and the catastrophe not yet arrived, Graham began teaching an evening course at Columbia on security analysis. It filled with working men from downtown offices who had never been offered a method before. One of them, a young instructor named David Dodd, took such careful notes that Graham suggested they turn the notes into a book.

Security Analysis appeared in 1934, in the pit of the depression, which is the right year for it. It is a heavy, technical, unglamorous volume, and it did something no book had done. It set out procedures. How to read a balance sheet with suspicion. How to test whether reported earnings are real. How to value a bond by asking what happens in the bad year rather than the average one.

It also contained the sentence people remember. In the short run the market is a voting machine, but in the long run it is a weighing machine. Votes are cast on fashion, fear and gossip. Weight is a matter of earnings, assets and dividends, and it asserts itself eventually, with no regard for how long you can wait.

The hardest idea in the book is net current asset value. Take a company's cash, its receivables and its stock, subtract every liability, and ignore the factories and the goodwill entirely. If the whole company can be bought for less than two thirds of that number, you are buying the business for less than its own loose change. In the 1930s there were hundreds of them.

Graham taught that course for nearly thirty years. The people who sat in it went on to run a surprising share of American money, and the whole profession of securities analysis grew out of those evenings, when a man who had just lost most of his clients' money stood up and explained how to count.

b: Security Analysis was for professionals. In 1949 Graham published the book he is now known for, The Intelligent Investor, and wrote it for the ordinary person with savings and no intention of becoming an analyst. Warren Buffett later called it simply the best book on investing ever written.

Its genius is one invented character. Imagine, Graham says, that you own a private business with a partner named Mister Market. Every single day this partner turns up and names a price at which he will buy your stake or sell you his. Some days he is cheerful and the price is high. Some days he is frightened about nothing in particular and the price is absurdly low. He never takes offence, and he has no idea what the business is worth.

You are not obliged to trade with him. His prices are an opportunity and never an instruction. The moment you let his mood tell you what your own property is worth, you have handed a manic depressive the keys to your life savings.

From that image everything practical follows. Graham divides readers into two kinds. The defensive investor wants a decent result with no trouble, so he holds a spread of solid companies and high grade bonds, never less than a quarter and never more than three quarters in either, rebalancing mechanically so that falling prices force him to buy and rising prices force him to sell. The enterprising investor will do real work for a better result, and must actually do it rather than merely feel enterprising.
And in the final chapter he condenses the whole book into three words. Margin of safety. Not forecasting, not timing, not brilliance. Pay a price that leaves you room to be wrong.
The book's deepest claim is one he repeats in various forms throughout. The investor's chief problem, and his worst enemy, is almost always himself.

b: There is an awkward fact at the heart of Graham's record, and to his credit he wrote about it himself rather than letting someone else find it.

In 1948 the Graham-Newman Corporation bought half of a small motor insurer called Government Employees Insurance Company, later GEICO, for a little over seven hundred thousand dollars. It broke his own rules twice over. It was far too large a share of the fund in one holding, and the case for it rested not on the balance sheet but on the quality of the business and the way it sold policies directly to careful drivers. Regulators then obliged the firm to hand the shares out to its investors rather than keep them.

Those shares went on to be worth more than every other profit Graham-Newman made in its entire history combined. An investor holding a hundred shares of the fund in 1948 who simply kept the GEICO distribution would have been sitting on well over a million dollars by the early 1970s. Graham noted the irony plainly. One decision taken partly outside his own system outperformed a lifetime of disciplined bargain hunting.

The other thing that came out of those years was a person. In 1950 a nineteen year old from Omaha sat in Graham's class at Columbia and earned the only top grade Graham is known to have given. Graham then declined to hire him, and the young man offered to work for nothing and was still turned down. Warren Buffett joined Graham-Newman in 1954 and stayed until Graham wound the firm up and retired in 1956.

Graham-Newman had compounded at roughly twenty per cent a year for two decades against about twelve for the market. Graham was sixty two, and had already decided that making money was the least interesting thing he knew how to do.
ch.cap: One rule broken outearns a lifetime of bargains

b: Graham spent his last twenty years in California and the south of France, teaching occasionally at the University of California in Los Angeles, translating poetry, writing a memoir, and losing a grown son.

Then, a few months before he died, he said something that still annoys people who make a living from his name. Asked by the Financial Analysts Journal in 1976 whether the detailed work of security analysis still paid, he answered that he was no longer an advocate of elaborate techniques of security analysis. He now preferred a highly simplified approach applying one or two tests to the price, and the test he liked best was paying no more than seven times the last twelve months of reported earnings, across a wide group of companies, sold by a mechanical rule.

He even allowed, to a very limited extent, that he was now on the side of the efficient market academics. The man who invented the profession was saying it had grown crowded enough to compete away most of its own advantage, and that an ordinary saver was better served by a simple rule faithfully followed than by clever judgement erratically applied.
He died at Aix-en-Provence on the twenty first of September 1976, aged eighty two.

Fifty years of research has treated the book roughly in places and kindly in others. The hunt for companies trading below their own cash largely died out in developed markets, because he taught too many people how to do it. Measures of cheapness based on book value are unreliable for firms whose real assets are software and brands rather than plant, and cheapness underperformed badly for much of the 2010s. The 2003 edition carries Jason Zweig's commentary precisely because many of Graham's thresholds no longer bite.

What has survived every test is the part he paid for personally. Price is a vote and value is a weight. Borrowed money converts a fall into a ruin. And no estimate, however careful, deserves to be acted on without room to be wrong.
ch.cap: A last rule: seven times earnings, no more

The Northern Pipe Line figures follow the Interstate Commerce Commission filings as reported in modern reconstructions of the campaign; the share counts and the seventy dollar distribution are well attested, while Graham's own valuation of about ninety five dollars is an estimate reconstructed from his method. recall: What did Graham's mother do in 1907, and what did it teach him?

She bought shares in United States Steel on margin, borrowing most of the purchase price, and was wiped out when prices collapsed in the Panic of 1907. Graham drew from it that leverage converts a temporary fall in price into a permanent loss of capital.
How did Graham find the Northern Pipe Line opportunity?

He read the company's annual filings in the Interstate Commerce Commission library in Washington in 1926, which pipelines were legally required to submit and almost nobody consulted. They showed idle railroad bonds making the shares worth far more than their price of about sixty two dollars.
How much did Graham's Joint Account fall from 1929, and why so badly?

It lost about seventy per cent from its peak over the years 1929 to 1932. He had bought genuinely cheap securities, but the account carried roughly forty four per cent margin debt, so falling prices forced losses before his analysis could be vindicated.
What is the Mister Market allegory?

Graham asks you to imagine a business partner who calls at your door every day with a price to buy your stake or sell you his, cheerful one day and terrified the next. His quotes are an opportunity, never an instruction about what your holding is worth.
What did Graham say in his 1976 interview with the Financial Analysts Journal?

He said he was no longer an advocate of elaborate techniques of security analysis and now preferred a highly simplified approach, favouring companies priced at no more than seven times the past twelve months of reported earnings, bought as a group and sold by a mechanical rule.
recap:
Benjamin Graham was born in London in 1894 and taken to New York as an infant. When he was nine his father died, the family's china importing business collapsed, and his mother took in lodgers to survive. Looking for a way back she borrowed money to buy shares in United States Steel on margin, and the Panic of 1907 wiped her out. Sent to the bank as a boy, Graham heard a teller ask aloud whether his mother was good for five dollars. Two lessons came out of that house. Borrowed money turns a temporary fall in price into a permanent loss. And a share of a steel company is a claim on the same business the day after a panic as the day before, so price and value are not the same thing.

He graduated from Columbia in 1914, second in his class, turned down teaching posts in three departments because he needed money, and went to work chalking prices in a brokerage for about twelve dollars a week. His edge was simple. He read the filings nobody read. In 1926, in a government library in Washington, he found a pipeline company whose shares cost about sixty two dollars while it sat on idle railroad bonds worth far more. His polite proposal at the 1927 meeting went unseconded. So he spent a year gathering proxies, arrived in 1928 with thirty eight per cent of the votes, won two board seats, and the company paid out seventy dollars a share.

Then the crash. Graham had bought cheap and done the analysis, but the account carried heavy margin debt, and from 1929 to 1932 it lost about seventy per cent. He worked without a profit share until his investors were whole. Out of that came margin of safety: buy at a price low enough that you can be wrong and still survive. He taught at Columbia for nearly thirty years, wrote Security Analysis in 1934, and in 1949 wrote The Intelligent Investor for ordinary savers. Its best invention is Mister Market, the partner who calls daily with a wildly varying price, whose quotes are an opportunity and never an instruction.

Months before his death in 1976 Graham said he no longer believed in elaborate analysis and preferred one simple rule faithfully applied. Which leaves one line worth keeping. Every price you are quoted is somebody's mood; what you are actually buying is what the thing earns and owns.
stories: Is she good for five dollars?

When Graham was a boy his father died and the family's china importing business died with him. His mother took in lodgers, then borrowed to buy United States Steel shares on margin, and the Panic of 1907 wiped her out. Sent to the bank to cash a cheque, young Benjamin stood at the window and heard the teller call over to the cashier, asking whether Dorothy Grossbaum was good for five dollars. He never forgot it. Fifty years later the most famous idea in investing, margin of safety, is really that boy's answer to that teller.

In 1926 Graham found a pipeline company in a government library whose shares cost about sixty two dollars while it quietly held railroad bonds worth far more. He bought two thousand of the forty thousand shares in existence and turned up at the 1927 annual meeting with a written proposal to hand the money back. Not one other shareholder would second his motion, so under the rules it could not even be read aloud, and the meeting closed. He spent the next year collecting proxies by post. In 1928 he arrived with thirty eight per cent of the votes, took two board seats, and the company paid out seventy dollars a share.
The rule he broke that made the money

In 1948 Graham's firm put a little over seven hundred thousand dollars into half of a small car insurer called GEICO. It broke his own rules: far too concentrated, and justified by the quality of the business rather than cheap assets. Regulators then forced the firm to distribute the shares to its investors. Those shares went on to earn more than every other profit in the firm's history put together. Graham said so himself, without flinching, which is a more useful thing than being consistent.
take: Price is a vote, value is a weight
Before you act on a number, ask whether it reflects what the thing earns and owns, or only what people currently feel about it. Write down your own estimate first, then look at the price.
Margin of safety is the whole method
Do not buy what is good; buy what is good at a price that survives your own mistakes. Decide in advance how wrong you can be and still be fine.
Borrowed money turns a dip into a ruin
Leverage removes your right to be patient. If a temporary fall can force you to sell, you do not really own the asset.
You are the main risk in your own portfolio
Graham thought temperament beat intellect. Build rules now, while calm, that will make the decision for you when you are not.
Graham's edge for twenty years was going to a public library and opening filings that were free to anyone. Boring primary data still beats confident opinion.
A share is a piece of a business, which entitles you to ask where the cash is and why it is sitting there. Apply the same question to your own company's accounts.
A mechanical rule beats unreliable judgement
Graham ended up preferring one simple test applied faithfully to elaborate analysis applied erratically. Choose the rule you will actually follow.

title: The Man Who Taught Wall Street to Count
wiifm: You already know that markets rise and fall. What you probably do not have is a defence against it. Graham built one out of childhood poverty, a proxy fight and a seventy per cent loss, then wrote it down in plain language for people with no interest in becoming analysts. By the end of this story you will know why price and value are different things, how to buy anything so that being wrong does not ruin you, and why the hardest part of handling money is not arithmetic but temperament. It is an hour that will quietly change how you read every price you are quoted.
